game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is fantastic.  It takes the themes expressed in Orwell's 1984 and allows you to take a "big brother" role by reading through social media to decide who is responsible for a series events thought to be done by terrorists.  I was on the edge of my seat the whole time, and it also made me think about every action I took.  Did I want to mark this suspect as potentially dangerous based on an altercation she got into a long time ago?  Is this article an accurate depiction of the person she is now?  Actions like these will come back to haunt you based on the outcomes later in the game.  

Overall, my only complaint with this game is that the ending felt a little too abrupt.  The game is episodic, and the final episode was significantly shorter than every other episode.  Overall, though, I would highly recommend picking this game up.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"The thoughts are free" ... or are they?

Orwell is a pretty neat little game about the potential dangers of openly accessible (or even not so openly accessible) data and the connections and conclusions you can draw from them.

You start out as an investigator for the project "Orwell", a surveillance system meant to protect the people and prevent crimes. 
After a bombing attack you are tasked, together with your supervisor, to find out who was behind the bombings and to prevent further ones.
As you dig deeper through websites and files, desktops and other material, you'll uncover more and more of the story, the motivations of the people responsible for the bombings and uncover some twists and turns throughout your investigations.

The gameplay is pretty simplistic. It's pretty much like surfing through a browser. You can access (predefined) websites and read through articles, blogs and also social media. Throughout the text you find some marked passages, which will help you with your investigation. You can connect these infos with a person and send these infos to Orwell. You can also decide to withhold some informations, letting events turn out differently in the process.

The story and events really sucked me in and were pretty thrilling. Slowly finding out more about the people, their connections to each other, and also be suprised by some twists, made the game very entertaining.

So if you don't mind simplistic gameplay and reading quite a lot and and the topic of data security doesn't turn you down, this is a little gem to keep an eye on.

I'd definitely recommend it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a fun, engaging, clever, brilliant, unique game that I would say is a mix of L.A. Noire, Her Story, Papers Please, and a touch of Telltale Games thrown in.

You go about solving a main crime which, along the way, you will discover a group of characters--all suspects. You do this by examining, accessing, reading through, and hacking into many different kinds of online resources (this would be the 'Her Story' aspect of it: A game where you get bits of the story unlocked, piece by piece and out of order, over time). As you go on, you will learn more and more about the suspects and characters and you need to try to figure out what information is relevant and what is not. What points of info is truth and what is false. What bits of knowledge and writings and conjectures are sarcasm or jokes and what is being said with true belief.... (the LA Noire side of it). Can you read between the lines and use logic and intuition to decide what will help you with the case and what may NOT be so smart to share with the database?

I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go. 

Orwell is [b]NOT[/b] going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try. 

[u]What's it about?[/u]

It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.

[u]Right. It's a game, so what's the gameplay like?[/u]

The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself. 

[u]Multiple choices. Does that mean there's a lot of replayability?[/u]

Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime. [b]BUT[/b] I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.

Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
A surprisingly immersive psuedo-visual novel that plays on the tropes of governmental surveillance in a way that makes you question every action that you make in the game. The writing is absolutely try-hard sometimes, to the point of being cringey only on rare occasions, but the overall story is interesting and captivating in a way that kept me on the edge of my seat the whole way through. You really begin to feel that you are an investigator, prying into the personal life of these people, and for a game so simple to do that is absolutely fantastic imo.

The mechanics are simple point, click, drag. The gameplay itself requires deducing events and character motivation through the combination of various news sources, emails, and hacked text messages. It requires a lot of reading and more thinking than I anticipated, leaving me stumped a few more times than I care to admit, but it doesn't feel boring in the slightest.

It's short, it's sweet, and it's to the point. I would recommend it to anyone that likes narrative experiences.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"[i]For how could you establish even the most obvious fact when there existed no record outside your own memory?[/i]"

Anybody who has read through George Orwell's [i]1984[/i] will recognize many prevolent themes throughout this point-and-click adventure. While many movies and games struggle to rival their literary counterparts, Orwell does a spectacular job of demonstrating the themes prevelant in George Orwell's story. While the actual story of the game is different from the book, focusing on the player rather than Winston, many of the aspects are still the same.

I only had a few minor gripes with Orwell that did not take too much away from the story or my immersion. The only real problem that I had with the game was the fact that you had to open each file up to add data to them, rather than just dragging and dropping them onto the character web.

A compelling story with many twists leaves the player hungry for more, available through multiple playthroughs of the game. A second season to Orwell would be very difficult to achieve, due to the ending of the game. I will not go into depth about what this is, as I cannot without spoiling the game.

I strongly reccomend you play through Orwell if you have read the novel [i]1984[/i] or are interested in games with themes of censorship and/or a malleable story.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! 

[h1] Overall Rating [/h1]
[b] WIP, FIS, IIS
2+2=5/6 [/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
In the wake of a recent bombing, someone needs to be tasked to help investigate the suspected bombers. That someone is you. You are in charge of what goes in the system and what doesn't. But is there more to it? Is there a group planning it all together, or just one person? Do you paint them as terrorists or do you leave out enough information to show them as innocent?

[h1]Welcome to Orwell[/h1]
Orwell is one of those stories that is best to go blind in, since it is the most effective the first time. Hearing or seeing anything that is related to the main story, especially the end, ruins how you would play. But why? You are playing yourself, a new recruit of a programed named Orwell tasked to investigate suspicious people regarding the recent bombing. Through, which I wished happened more, a cutscene perfectly showing why and what this game is with only visuals. If you read 1984 Orwell is similar to how the government watches their people as it was influenced from George Orwell's books.

[h1]Datachunk Uploaded[/h1]
Down to it's core, you only read highlighted items, or datachunks, and dragging them to profiles for uploading. But there is much more if you are willing. Datachunks are meant to be evaluated, is this noteworthy to put on someone's profile? Do you purposefully make someone look worse or better? Should you upload every little thing? The game tried to put you in this mindset by your supervisor's comments and by conflicting datachunks (represented by a yellow highlight) to show you can't upload every little thing. Of course, there are datachunks needed to continue. Most of the time it is very apparent the datachunk is needed as it gives something new you can look through, solve a conflicting datachunk, or a sound cue picks up. This is all combined to represent how you view the situation. How you view the people you were tasked to investigate. How you have an influence on how their life will go after Orwell injected you into their lives. Sure, they do make their own decisions, but you have the power to have them forever be seen as a threat by the government.

Your first playthrough is key. It is how you would react in this situation, not how some character would. You do not know anything except what you gather. All other playthroughs after that is to see what could have happened if you did something differently. Anything you know about the main storyline ruins how you make decisions in the game. So I do recommend knowing as little as possible to get the most out of it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a thought-provoking narrative simulation developed by Osmotic Studios and published by Daedalic Entertainment that places the player in the uncomfortable role of a government surveillance operative. Rather than offering power fantasies or conventional heroism, the game asks you to sit behind a screen, analyze fragments of people’s digital lives, and decide which pieces of information deserve official attention. Set in the fictional state known simply as The Nation, the story unfolds in the aftermath of a violent terrorist attack, where fear, public pressure, and political urgency justify the rapid expansion of a system capable of monitoring nearly every aspect of a citizen’s existence.

The central mechanic revolves around the Orwell surveillance system itself, a sleek but unsettling interface through which you access emails, chat logs, social media profiles, news articles, phone records, and private files. Gameplay consists of identifying relevant “datachunks” and uploading them into official investigation dossiers. What makes this process compelling is that not all information is equally meaningful, nor is it always truthful when stripped of context. A casual message, a sarcastic comment, or an old association can become damning evidence once formalized inside the system. The act of choosing what to submit becomes the game’s primary decision-making tool, transforming seemingly mundane interactions into high-stakes moral choices.

Narratively, Orwell unfolds across multiple in-game days, each representing a new phase of the investigation and introducing fresh characters, revelations, and complications. The pacing is deliberate, allowing tension to build gradually as threads intertwine and suspects emerge. Rather than presenting clear villains and heroes, the story thrives on ambiguity. Individuals under scrutiny are complex, flawed, and often sympathetic, and the more you learn about them, the more uncomfortable the process of surveillance becomes. The game excels at showing how partial truths can snowball into irreversible consequences, especially when filtered through institutional authority.

A defining strength of Orwell is its ethical focus. The game consistently challenges the player to reflect on the power they wield and the ease with which that power can be misused. Uploading information feels procedural and routine, yet the consequences are often deeply personal for the people affected. Careers are ruined, relationships collapse, and lives spiral based on decisions made in silence behind a terminal. The game does not present clear “right” answers; instead, it forces players to confront the reality that surveillance systems are shaped as much by human judgment and bias as by data itself.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist, utilitarian aesthetic that reinforces its themes. Interfaces resemble real-world operating systems and investigative software, grounding the experience in plausibility rather than spectacle. This stripped-down presentation keeps attention focused on text, decisions, and implications rather than visual distraction. Sound design is similarly restrained, using subtle cues rather than dramatic music to maintain an atmosphere of quiet tension and bureaucratic detachment. The result is an experience that feels unsettling precisely because of how ordinary and believable it is.

Player agency is a key component of the experience, though it is intentionally constrained. While the overarching investigation follows a structured path, the specific outcomes depend heavily on what information you choose to reveal or withhold. Multiple endings and branching consequences encourage replayability, as players can explore how different ethical approaches alter the narrative. Some may approach the game as a dutiful analyst focused solely on public safety, while others may attempt to protect individual privacy whenever possible. Each approach reveals different facets of the story and reinforces the game’s central question: who decides what is justified when security and freedom collide?

Reception to Orwell has been consistently positive, particularly among players who value narrative depth and social commentary. Many praise its relevance, especially in an era defined by data collection, algorithmic profiling, and online identity. While some may find the gameplay slow or limited due to its text-heavy nature, those willing to engage with its pacing often find it deeply immersive and emotionally resonant. The lack of traditional action is not a weakness but a deliberate design choice that underscores the quiet, insidious nature of surveillance.

Ultimately, Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You stands as a powerful example of how games can explore modern societal issues with nuance and restraint. It transforms data analysis into a dramatic and morally charged experience, reminding players that information is never neutral and that those who control it shape reality itself. For players interested in narrative-driven games that challenge assumptions and provoke reflection rather than offer escapism, Orwell delivers a memorable and unsettling journey that lingers long after the screen goes dark.

Rating: 8/10

First played it in 2016 and got the bad ending. Decided to return to it again today and try for real this time. Completely worth it.
The story is excellent. Just when you thought you got to the bottom of it, it pulls the rug under your feet and goes even deeper. Several times i was sure i deduced everything and solved the mystery, and every time new information appeared and made me completely rethink everything. By the end it forms a messy web, yet i could see through it a coherent story and everything made sense. The whole thing is just very immersive.
Here, like in many story driven games, the gameplay is just a tool to deliver the plot, and the only thing that really matters is if it does it well without being too distracting. This may be up to personal taste, but i found it enjoyable enough that i didn't feel bored at any moment. Reading through articles and text conversations looking for useful data and following the story was engaging. Though i suppose if you don't enjoy too much reading in games it might get monotonous inbetween the story segments.
Overall would recommend it, especially if you're looking for a good engaging story.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Short, simple and yet so very much worth it.[/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] places the player in a role of an investigator for a mass surveillance system of the same name. After being assigned a case, the investigator's job is to gather information related to it using means provided by the system - relevant websites, private chats and so on. Information gathered is passed along to an 'adviser' who provides feedback and proceeds with other actions if necessary.

[u]The gameplay itself is rather simplistic.[/u] Shortly put, it consists of a lot of reading and putting highlighted information into the system (with a mere hold'n'drag method), though some of the data may conflict with each other and it will be up to the player to decide which information is correct. I do agree with those who say that [u]the mechanics could be improved[/u], as there is only a small amount of any form of detective work for the player to perform and some may feel like their hand is being held way too often. I should definitely mention though that [u]your choices do matter and influence the story.[/u]

Since I have mentioned it, it would be unforgivable not to say that [u]I found the story incredibly engaging[/u]. The [u]high-level of character development[/u] kept on working me over and over, changing how I feel about specific characters, making me alternate between love and hate for them, leading me on thinking I might have figured out the bad guy only to be presented an even more attractive suspect. 
One bad thing about it? [u]I completed the game in about four hours[/u], which is a liiittle bit short..

[u]The art style itself is very appealing, something which can also be said about the soundtrack[/u] (though do keep in mind it's meant to serve as background music - don't expect high energy or colourfulness!)

I don't think I would be too far off if I called [i]Orwell[/i] a novel which slowly unfolds itself before the player. In my opinion [u]it is a really great experience[/u] and [b]the developers released a demo version[/b] - make sure to play it to see if the game is for you! If you still have your doubts, which are very much understandable due to the simplistic gameplay, consider getting it on sale. It's worth it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Remember when we were all shocked by the Snowden leaks a few years ago? Ever wanna play at being the NSA trying to stop a terrorist threat?

PROS:
+Simple gameplay, but still fun.
+Take part in uncovering a deep and interconnected web of investigation.
+Lots of morally gray areas.
+Philosophically intriguing.
+Politically potent.
+While you investigate, you are sometimes forced to make decisions without a wider understanding, and hope you made the right call. It's crushing when you find out that you made a mistake.
+Excellent soundtrack!
+A calm, peaceful aesthetic clashes with the dark subject matter in the perfect way.
+Definitely rewards taking your time to read through everything going on, with lots of little tidbits to help tell the whole story. Worth additional playthroughs.
+A world which feels truly lived-in, from the news to the social media to the characters.
+Your choices matter, and there's multiple, distinct endings which feel different from eachother when you look at the end result.

CONS:

review_text_raw:
[h1]A must-play for any cyber-security enthusiast[/h1]

[i]Received this as a gift from a dear friend[/i]

[b]Note:[/b]

Playing this game involves a lot of reading and if that's not your thing, you're probably not gonna enjoy Orwell.
But if you like playing VN's, I believe you'll love it!

[b]Gameplay:[/b]

You're an investigator in a secret mass-surveillance program run by the government, called Orwell (named after [url=https://youtu.be/h9JIKngJnCU]George Orwell, author of the novel '1984'[/url]).
Your job is to read up the information in your [i]Reader[/i] and upload [i]chunks[/i] of it to the Orwell database.
Uploading certain information may open up more leads and you may get unrestricted access to the 'target' person's PC, mobile, medical records and what not.

At certain times, you may find conflicting bits of information.
At such times, it's best to avoid resolving the issue. Read other relevant details and when you come back, it'd be clear to you what the right information is.

During the entire course of the game, all you do is read - a person's social network feed, their blogs. Sometimes you tap their calls and messages. But, you never directly interact with the individuals.
Yet, you gain so much knowledge about them that you practically know the person. Without actually [i]knowing[/i] them.
And all that just in the timeframe of 5 days!
It's kinda amazing and disturbing at the same time.

Also, the most important thing. Once an information is uploaded to Orwell, it cannot be deleted.
And there could be consequences depending on what you upload.
So, you wanna be careful, to not wrongly accuse an innocent. Which, trust me, is not that easy.

[b]My thoughts:[/b]
[i](May contain SPOILERS. Or it may simply affect your experience of the game. So read at your own risk ¯\_(ツ)_/¯ )[/i]

I loved the game.
Government mass surveillance has been a topic of concern for quite some time now.
It was ingenious to make a game that puts the player on the opposite side of the coin where the player is the one carrying out the surveillance.

At first, while it's all new and sunny, you feel like an unrivaled God - passing righteous judgments, punishing the wrong-doers. That is what you're made to believe you are.
And you find all sorts of crazy, unstable people in the world that you feel they [i]need[/i] to be surveilled.
Then you find out that they had a disturbing past that made them into what they are.
Then you realize that passing righteous judgments is a lot more difficult than you had initially assumed. And that personal data is a sensitive thing and it can destroy lives. And that YOU might be destroying someone's life as a part of your [i]work[/i].
If you're lucky, you'll wake up in time and realize how faulty the system is. And how you've been probing into other's personal lives and just how despicable that really is.
Otherwise, you either lose your humanity forever and become a Dementor that feeds on other people's personal lives. Or you go insane. Or both.

Maybe this journey of realization is similar to the one Edward Snowden had. Only, his journey was real and his actions had real consequences.
I would strongly recommend anyone to watch [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt3774114/]Snowden[/url] and [url=http://www.imdb.com/title/tt4044364/]Citizenfour[/url] after playing the game if you haven't already.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
If you like to exercise your mind, this is a game for you. If you like to be nosy or adore crime thriller, this is also the game for you. Orwell really teases your brain and forces you to keep track of your steps as you're made to retrace them again and again.

If you don't like milling through data and tasks that require you be VERY thorough and thoughtful, this game is not for you. You will find it boring. Although a lot of fun, I can easily see how one might find this boring. This is truly an NSA simulator--you're rifling thorugh data, and tons of it. If you're not one to hunker down and read through information, you'll either get stuck or choose a wrong path. The game is linear in its structure...some choices can send you down different paths but the idea stays the same. I've only finished one playthrough but it's clear when you can take things down a different path.As with true research, you can waste plenty of time collecting incessant things or even collect incorrect information. Your selections DO effect the story and have consequences, similar to the ones you might evoke in real life. You cannot change them, even immediately afterwards. This game has a lot of replay potential as each chapter can deviate significantly as you fill in the holes.

There were two instances where the game requires you to input 'useless' or 'false' information in order to progress, which threw me off as most of the game revolves around you putting down as much 'accurate' info as possible.

I truly enjoy how thought provoking Orwell is...I'm not easily emotionally swayed by games, but I legitimately recieved goosebumps during one chapter, where the realizations of what this game implies about government and observation truly sank in....of how surveillance can provide extremes pulled from both the good and the bad.

Not a game for everyone, but an excellent, easygoing and extremely thought-provoking game all the same. I like visual novels and puzzles, but I'm picky as I have a short attention span and am a bit of a snob when it comes to the quality of the plot and writing of the story....I am tempted to play it again, just to see where my choices take me. This rarely happens. I just bought the sequel... 7/10

review_text_raw:
I believe Fellow Traveller Games is very interested in making people switch to Tails with giving away their published "Linux basics" game Hacknet for free (multiple times even!) first, and now give away this game too to fuel your paranoia and use some of that know-how to make you try and hide.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.
There is no way to change the font neither through options nor through config files, forum searches gave nothing in regards to that either, so be mindful of that.

Firstly this is a visual novel, so no super exciting and engaging gameplay is to be found, but honestly that may be for the better in these spying games.

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]About the Game[/h1]
Orwell is a game in which you have to read through articles, conversations and the likes to find bits of information to uncover a terrorist act. Depending on which information you present or withold, your superiors gain a different image of a person - which in turn can affect the outcome of the story.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
If you expect action-packed run'n'gun gameplay, this game is not for you. Instead, try to see it more as a mystery/interactive puzzle game. You read through a person's Blog and try to understand their motivation. Suddenly, you realize that two people you were investigating had a connection to each other, and thus you delve deeper into the story.

[h1]Theme / Story[/h1]
It couldn't be more relevant or timely. The game touches subjects like terrorism, state surveillance, how much information we present of ourselves or how much power the state should have. I enjoyed the perspective of "The Man" very much, as usually these dystopian futures are experienced through resistance fighters (because guns!).

[h1]Would I recommend it?[/h1]
Yes and no. First of all, if you are one of those "This isn't a game"-people, you just won't have fun with it.
Second, if you are anxious to make the "wrong" choice in a game (like me, for instance - [i]Datachunk marked[/i]), then this game might be troublesome for you.

You see, I tend to play these games like this: First, I select which outcome I want to achieve (e.g. save person X) and then act how I believe this outcome can be achieved.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I'm surprised how lukewarm a lot of the reviews of this game are - I thought it was phenomenal! I guess it's because the game is mostly reading?

The government has created a piece of software designed to spy on anyone and everyone with the aim of catching criminals and terrorists. You are recruited as an investigator tasked with using it to create profiles of suspicious individuals, going through their emails, phones, desktops, etc... aiming to find anything incriminating.

Although it might seem obvious that an all-powerful piece of spying software may be somewhat unethical, Orwell does a great job at making you [i]experience[/i] it. When you're listening in on a suspect's phone call and rather than anything incriminating you just hear an argument between a couple going through a hard time in their relationship, you feel kinda gross. When you label somebody as angry and hateful based on a blog post they wrote years ago, which you later found out they regret, you get a pit in your stomach realising that the profile you made of them could have a big negative impact on this person's life in the future.

Saying that, the game doesn't feel preachy. You [i]are[/i] able to use the software to hunt down and reveal criminals who may have otherwise gone scot-free, and the game makes it clear that increased surveillance [i]is[/i] leading to dramatic reductions in crime. So does that make the gross invasion of privacy ultimately justified?? I really enjoyed how conflicted I felt up to the very end and how much it made me think.

This is a game where your choices really do matter, different people may live, die, or be arrested in your playthrough based on the choices that you make. I actually replayed the final chapter a second time because I wasn't satisfied with my ending, and managed to unlock a lot of extra information I didn't get the first time. 

I was super gripped the whole way through and am excited to play the sequel now!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Finished in 3 hours, did not replay to look for alternate choices.

You play as a character who works for the government and has complete access to internet, phone calls, text messages, etc. Your job is to investigate people, collect evidence, and solve (and prevent) terrorist crimes. You're the man behind the camera in the all-seeing surveillance state. 

The way the surveillance system is set up is that you collect the information and pass it to an analyst. The analyst looks at the information and decides whether it is sufficient to arrest somebody, or enough to indicate another person is a person of interest that you're allowed to investigate. Over time the network of people you're investigating grows, and it's harder to keep track of their history and relationionships.

If you collect the correct information, you might be able to prevent terrorist attacks. It is possible to get enough evidence to arrest people who aren't actually dangerous or ringleaders.

Sometimes, you see conflicting information (such as when one person is lying) and you need to make a decision. You can't submit both pieces of evidence, you can't delete evidence once you've submitted it (silly, but a game mechanic to make your choices more meaningful), and sometimes it's not clear which one is correct. You sometimes can dig around and find out which piece is correct, but sometimes you need to go with your gut and what you think the people's motivations are. 

Other times, it's not clear that you're making a choice. You can always choose to submit or not submit information, and it could lead to different results. The only way to know this is to replay the game and deliberately not choose things that led to bad outcomes. At first I was just grabbing and submitting all the information I saw, but you're intended to put a bit more thought into it. Is this relevent information? Do you want the analyist making a decision based on this information? Is this quote being taken out of context? Are you encouraging your analyist to arrest a harmless person?

My only complaint about the game is [spoiler] there is only one case/group you get to investigate, and that investigation turns "meta" at the end -- having discovered the ORWELL system you're using to spy on them, they start interacting with you directly. I kind of wanted to see the system working as intended for a few cases before the "finale" case where your subjects figure out what's going on.[/spoiler] I know it's a smaller indie type of game, but a few more cases to establish what you're doing, how significant your choices are, and so on BEFORE it reached that point would have been appreciated.

I did enjoy this game. It involves a lot of reading, and a lot of thinking, in order to enjoy it properly. It's not a good game for people who want to click through the boring stuff to get to the exciting part. In a way, it's more akin to the visual novel genre than it is to more traditional games.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell was an interesting experience, with a lot of potential and promise. I will say that I did enjoy the game for the most part, however, there are some glaring details which ruined it for me. 

The game relies on you (the investigator) uploading particular parsed sections of text to the server (Orwell), which means that whenever you come across a piece of information which is a "trigger" for want of a better term, it is highlighted - regardless of its relivence (and some information is totally surplus to requirement, a lot in one case). This means that most of the information which you read through, including important plot points, or interesting backstory, is largely irrelivent and the player (or at least I did) found myself just slowly scrolling to the bottom of every document to highlight all the options before I read anything at all. This is especially clear when investigating information which contradicts other information which has not been disclosed yet (marked by yellow highlighting instead of blue), as it will always be yellow, even if you have access to but haven't discovered the other piece of information yet - which unless the investigator is psychic, makes zero sense. A shame, since this dulls enthusiasm for what could otherwise be an engaging plot.

While processing this information you are presented with multiple occasions where information would be important to the case, but you cannot add it to your current file or create a new file because the game is not ready for you to do so. You will then later come back to re-read and submit this data after the game tells you the information you already noticed is important. This is irritating and makes the player feel like mommy is holding their hand through the entire experience, rather than allowing them to work on their own initiative. Although on reflection, this is most likely because the order in which the data is presented to you is not well organised from a storytelling perspective.

Attention to detail is somewhat lacking for a detective game also, as on multiple occasions you are directed to a forum which is occasionally updated with new articles to peruse. Unfortunately, when these articles are "published" the game does not update the "last logged in" sections of the user's profiles, which creates confusion over the timeline [spoiler]especially since this becomes important later in the story[/spoiler].

However, the largest problem is that there are several key events which the game does not provide you enough information to correctly answer (and there is a correct answer), which leads to the player essentially taking a wild guess as to which of the options is the correct one. If you are fortunate, you will get the result which you were looking for - if not... well you'll have to go through the entire game again from the beginning, as the game auto-saves after every piece of information you upload.

Overall, Orwell is a thought-provoking and mostly enjoyable game, but it does have it's flaws. If you can overlook them however, you will appreciate the intention of the developer. At this point I have to decide if I recommend Orwell or not, and it is difficult... 

8/10. Would not play again.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Hoooo boy. How to start.

Orwell is absolutely Orwellian, but for any literature nerds like me out there, this isn't like an adaptation of 1984 or Animal Farm or even Homage to Catalonia. But The Nation, the central society that the game takes place in, is an Orwellian state. Someone's always watching. In this case, it's you. An act of terror has been committed, and it's up to you to sift through blogs, emails, telephone calls, texts, photos, even remote-accessing citizen's computers in order to find out whodunnit. Esentially, you ARE Big Brother. Similarly to Papers, Please, you work for the system. But that's where the similarities stop because Orwell is visually stunning, with an intuitive interface and in-your-face consequences for your actions.

I've played every dystopian, utopian, cyberpunk, post-cyberpunk, pre-cyberpunk, and anything that even sounds like cyberpunk game I could get my hands on, and this is easily in the top five percent. Orwell allows you the freedom to choose what kind of observer/reporter you'll be. Will you try your best to do what's right by the Nation? Will you use your position on the inside to help the resistance? The choices can be subtle - I found myself making honest mistakes, people going to prison who didn't deserve it or worse. And what's equally intriguing as what's in Orwell is what is implied - the type of society you're observing, her inhabitants. There's a lot of reading, but it establishes a base for a complex and interesting world. If I had to fault it, it would be on replayability. You're allowed to explore so much and the resolution is so memorable that I can't imagine being as surprised again. Even so, I immensely enjoyed my playthrough.

Orwell was worth every cent I paid for it. In fact, it's one of the best games I've played this year. It was beautiful, engaging, and timely. You won't regret playing it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a gripping techno-thriller about the consequences of mass surveillance.

In the game, you take on the role of an "Investigator" and soon find yourself tasked with using the mass surveillance system "Orwell" to uncover the perpetrators behind a terrorist attack. However, things soon become a lot more complicated as you creep through the private lives of seemingly innocent citizens, trawling through their social media accounts, phone calls and even private files in an effort to uncover evidence.

From a gameplay perspective, Orwell is very much what I would call an "interactive story". You'll be doing a lot of reading, but the writing is excellent and the feeling of doing detective work will keep you hooked. This is very much the game equivalent of a page-turner.

I don't want to spoil the story, so suffice to say that I found it highly engaging and I was interested all the way through to the end. Not only that, but there are several places in the game where your decisions weigh unusually heavily and will affect the outcome of the story. Finally, the game gives an eerie look into a not-so distant future where we are under the watchful eye of a mass surveillance system. In this day and age of interconnectedness, the plot of Orwell is disturbingly believable.

During my time with Orwell I experienced a few technical issues, including slowdowns and glitches that required ALT+F4:ing out of the game and restarting it. These disruptions did detract a bit from the overall impression of the game, but not much.

All in all, I highly recommend Orwell. If you enjoyed "Papers, Please" I'm sure you will enjoy Orwell.
